BBC, 24 Nov 2026

Women's concerns about asylum not racist, says think tank

Human rights and equality barrister Dr Anna Loutfi has raised concerns about the impact of mass migration on women

Woman with short dark hair stands in front of Houses of Parliament. It is evening and she is wearing a black jacket and a cream pullover. She is standing on a grassy area with trees and street lights behind.

The government has been accused of a \"dereliction of its duty to protect citizens\" by allowing a planned asylum centre.

The shadow minister for women and equalities, Joy Morrisey, said Labour had ignored warnings raised by residents and police when it granted permission for the redevelopment of part of MoD Bicester in Oxfordshire.

She was speaking at the launch of a think tank report called Mass Immigration is a Women's Issue, attended by women from Piddington, a village near the military site.

The Home Office said other large sites had been operating for a number of years with no rising crime. The Refugee Council said \"there is no evidence refugees commit crimes...more than any other groups\".

But the report's author, human rights and equality barrister Dr Anna Loutfi, said the government has not disclosed data on how crime rates change when large-scale male encampments are created.

That is backed by a University of Oxford Migration Observatory report from August 2026 that said there is no published data on convicted offenders' immigration status, such as whether they are an asylum seeker, refugee, work migrant or international student.

Piddington villagers voted overwhelmingly to become an independent state in a symbolic referendum

Some villagers in Piddington - home to 350 people, including 133 women - have said they will be living in fear if 1,256 male asylum seekers are housed nearby.

Planning permission for the MoD Bicester site was approved by the Housing Secretary Angela Rayner earlier this month after the Home Office used a fast-track route for projects deemed to be urgently needed and of national importance.

It said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.

Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site, which has also been legally challenged by campaigners.

A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against and one in support.

Loutfi said the concerns they were raising were common sense: \"Even if this was a group of football fans it would be of concern.

\"But these men often come from countries where there are culturally incompatible ways of viewing women, they're viewed as available if they are unaccompanied or dressed a certain way or drinking alcohol.

\"Most of the men are single, young, excitable with nothing to do all day, it doesn't take a rocket scientist to see putting a large number of them into a population of a lot less women will be trouble.\"

Essex Police covers the area around MDP Wethersfield which has been used to house 800 single male migrants since 2023.

The Chief Constable of the force said in September that crime linked to the site is \"very low\" with 15 offences since it opened in which a member of the public was the victim and the suspect was identified as, or alleged to be, a Wethersfield \"service user\".

Imran Hussain, Director of External Affairs at the Refugee Council, said: \"Violence against women and girls is a problem across society that needs to be addressed to ensure that people feel safe in their homes and communities.

\"But public debate and narratives must reflect the fact that there is no evidence refugees commit crimes towards women and girls more than any other groups.\"

Women from Piddington met with Baroness Davies of Devonport - Olympic swimmer Sharron Davies - after their meeting in the House of Lords

The Women's Policy Centre, that commissioned Loufi's report, is an independent think tank. It invited MPs from all political parties to the launch of the report and said the issue of mass immigration and women's safety is a cross party issue.

Sandra Innes, a Piddington resident of 23 years, said she felt the government was being \"hugely naive\" in stating that the chance of crime was negligible.

She said women in the village were \"living on the edge\" and said their huge frustration was the lack of communication from ministers.

\"Why isn't someone coming to us engaging and talking about how they will safeguard us?\" she added.

The Home Office has said it is working closely with local authorities, police, health partners and community representatives to ensure any impact is carefully managed and local concerns are addressed.

In the conditions of planning permission, it said the site would be closely managed through 24-hour staffing, controlled access, CCTV and security patrols which would \"reduce\" the risk.

In August, the government created a nine-page booklet for asylum seekers explaining rape, sexual harassment and domestic abuse are illegal in the UK and giving guidance on how UK laws and customs may be different from their home countries.

Up to 1,256 men could be housed at the site near Bicester under the plans

Reform's Fareham and Waterlooville MP Suella Braverman attended the meeting.

She is the party's spokesperson on equalities and said she was concerned to see campaigners in Piddington accused of racism on social media for voicing concerns about the development.

\"It is not racist to want to keep women and girls safe. Just recently we have seen an Iranian migrant arrested in Crowborough (another former military site being used to house migrants).

\"That is coming to Piddington unless the government changes course and listens to the women,\" she added.

Sussex Police has confirmed a 20 year old Iranian man living in Crowborough was arrested following a report of indecent exposure on 10 November but did not confirm if that man is an asylum seeker.

But Hussain said: \"Toxic rhetoric against refugees and people in the asylum system doesn't make women safer — it simply dehumanises people who have fled war and terror, many of whom are themselves survivors of oppressive regimes like the Taliban or of sexual violence.\"

Planning documents state that those living on the MoD Bicester site would be free to enter and leave and that \"the site's relatively isolated location and limited pedestrian connections are likely to constrain journeys on foot\".

It added that the measures cannot eliminate \"all risk\", but officials consider they would \"materially reduce\" security and community safety risks.

Liberal Democrat MP Calum Miller, who represents the area, said he understands the concerns from the women about the impact on their daily lives: \"It is why I have been asking Home Office ministers to ensure local services, including policing, have the resources they need to keep people safe.\"

The minister for border security and asylum, Anna Turley, said there is \"a target\" for work to start on the centre in January with it becoming operational in April.

Further assessments and approvals are needed before a final decision to proceed is determined.
